title: Escalation sync: rollout regression + rollback safeguards (NorthBridge)
summary: Customer escalation follow-up after a model rollout regression caused elevated p95 latency and intermittent 5xx. NorthBridge recapped impact, gaps in current manual rollback process, and asked Redwood to provide automated rollback tied to latency/error SLOs with strong guardrails (min traffic, warm-up, cooldown, baseline comparison) and auditability. Redwood reviewed preliminary plan for auto-rollback on SLO breach, monitor requirements/labeling, and proposed a staged enablement starting with a single route/region in Dedicated.
topics: Incident recap: timeline, latency spike + 5xx during rollout
Why rollback didn’t happen quickly (signal + ownership + tooling)
Auto-rollback requirements: thresholds, windows, warm-up, cooldown, baseline compare
Monitoring dependencies: SLO definitions, monitor identity/labeling consistency
Safety: avoid flapping and multi-tenant cascading rollbacks
Audit logs, change history, and approvals/override
Staged rollout plan and next steps
next_steps: Redwood to share proposed auto-rollback policy defaults and UI mock (verdict + history) for feedback.
NorthBridge to confirm target SLO thresholds per tier/route and whether to use baseline compare for initial pilot.
Redwood SRE to validate NorthBridge monitors/labels (route/model/region/tier) and identify any missing metrics.
Schedule a pilot kickoff to enable auto-rollback for one canary route in us-east with a feature flag.
Redwood to send incident write-up summary + recommended monitor queries for NorthBridge to review.
action_items: Hannah Rivera - Send recap email with proposed rollout auto-rollback plan + ETA ranges - 2025-02-14
Rafael Mendes - Review NorthBridge latency/error SLO dashboards + confirm data freshness/lag expectations - 2025-02-18
Paula Mendes - Share draft policy semantics (min traffic, warm-up, cooldown, baseline compare) and collect customer feedback - 2025-02-20
Benji Okafor - Provide monitor identity/label checklist for route/model/region/tier to ensure controller can query correctly - 2025-02-18
Lena Wu (NorthBridge) - Provide the exact timestamps of customer-visible impact and current paging thresholds - 2025-02-14
Amit Desai (NorthBridge) - Confirm which routes and regions are in-scope for pilot + any change-management constraints - 2025-02-19

Fireflies.ai Transcript

Title: Escalation sync: rollout regression + rollback safeguards (NorthBridge)
Recorded: 2025-02-13 21:00 UTC
Duration: 48 min
Attendees:
- Hannah Rivera (Redwood Inference)
- Rafael Mendes (Redwood Inference)
- Paula Mendes (Redwood Inference)
- Benji Okafor (Redwood Inference)
- Amit Desai (NorthBridge Analytics)
- Lena Wu (NorthBridge Analytics)
- Carlos Jimenez (NorthBridge Analytics)
- Jenna Park (NorthBridge Analytics)

Summary (auto-generated): Discussed impact from recent model rollout latency regression, current rollback process, and safeguards needed to enable automatic rollback based on SLO breaches.

Topics (auto-generated): incident review, rollback policy, SLO monitors, audit logs, rollout guardrails, next steps.

Action items (auto-generated): Redwood to share draft policy + monitor labeling checklist; NorthBridge to confirm pilot scope and thresholds.


[00:00] Hannah Rivera: Okay. Cool. Folks are joining. Um, thanks everyone for hopping on. This is Hannah from Redwood. I’m on Customer Success for NorthBridge. I pulled in Rafael from SRE, Paula from Product, and Benji from the control plane team.

[00:14] Hannah Rivera: Goal today is really: let’s do the impact review from Tuesday’s rollout regression, and then align on what safeguards you need to feel good enabling auto-rollback when we ship it. Sound good?

[00:27] Amit Desai: Yep. Thanks Hannah. This has been… a fun week. (laughs) Appreciate you pulling the right people.

[00:34] Lena Wu: Yeah thanks. We have some pretty specific asks here.

[00:38] Hannah Rivera: Great. Amit, do you want to start with your view of impact and timeline? Then Rafael can fill in what we saw on our side.

[00:46] Amit Desai: Sure. So, Tuesday, around… I have it written down… 10:12 AM Pacific we started seeing p95 jump. We have an internal endpoint that hits you guys for chat completions. It went from like ~650ms p95 to 1.9 seconds, sometimes 2.4. And then we got intermittent 5xx, not constant, but enough to trip our own error budget alert.

[01:11] Carlos Jimenez: It also changed output length a bit? Like it started streaming later. But the big issue is latency.

[01:16] Amit Desai: Right. Latency, and the perception internally was “Redwood is down.” Even if you weren’t down-down.

[01:23] Hannah Rivera: Understood.

[01:24] Amit Desai: Our on-call escalated to me because it was during business hours and it affected one of our customer-facing workflows. We had to flip traffic back to the old model version. But that took… I don’t know, like 35 minutes end to end because we were trying to figure out if it was our VPC or yours, and then who had the lever to roll back.

[01:46] Lena Wu: I’ll add: we didn’t have a single “rollback now” button. It was: open a ticket, ping Slack, then go into our config, we were chasing which version was the canary. It’s too much when the graph is on fire.

[02:01] Hannah Rivera: Yeah. That’s painful. Rafael, can you confirm what we saw and where the delay was?

[02:08] Rafael Mendes: Yep. So from our side, we saw elevated request queue time in us-east Dedicated pool backing your deployment. There was also a bump in 502s. We correlated it to the rollout of model version… I’m gonna butcher it… “rb-instruct-13b-v7.2”? Something like that.

[02:25] Carlos Jimenez: That’s close. It’s the fine-tune. We call it NB-Assist-v7.2. It’s pinned to the base model, yes.

[02:33] Rafael Mendes: Right, sorry. The base runtime config changed. The rollout was a 10% canary at first, then ramped.

[02:41] Benji Okafor: It ramped to 35% automatically based on time, not based on SLO health. That’s the current limitation.

[02:48] Rafael Mendes: Exactly. Our current rollout controller doesn’t have “if latency is bad, rollback.” We had the dashboards showing it, but no automation.

[02:57] Hannah Rivera: And the timeline from our incident channel, we had an engineer engaged at… 10:24 PT, and the traffic split was reverted at 10:47 PT. So about 23 minutes from first page to revert.

[03:12] Lena Wu: And that’s after we pinged like three people.

[03:14] Hannah Rivera: Yeah.

[03:15] Jenna Park: For us the issue is, we have commitments around incident response and change control. If a rollout can degrade customer experience, we need deterministic behavior. Either it auto-reverts within a defined SLO window, or we need a formal approval gate. Right now it’s neither.

[03:32] Hannah Rivera: Totally fair.

[03:34] Paula Mendes: Hi, I’m Paula, I own rollout policy product side. The feature we’re building is specifically to reduce that time-to-rollback, while adding guardrails so it doesn’t “flap.” I can talk through the knobs and then we can see what matches your expectations.

[03:49] Amit Desai: Please.

[03:51] Paula Mendes: The short version: you define a rollback policy per route/model/region/tier. Policy includes: latency and error thresholds, evaluation windows, minimum request volume, a warm-up delay after a deploy starts, and then a cooldown after rollback triggers. Optionally: compare against baseline (previous stable version) so we only rollback if canary is worse than stable.

[04:19] Lena Wu: The baseline compare is important. We had a separate incident last month where overall region latency was high because of network, and we don’t want you to rollback just because the internet is bad.

[04:29] Rafael Mendes: Yep. That’s one of the guardrails we’re leaning on. But it depends on having both series available: canary and baseline. And labeling has to be clean.

[04:40] Benji Okafor: “Clean labeling” meaning: route, model version, region, and customer tier tags are consistent so the monitor query is actually the right time series.

[04:49] Carlos Jimenez: Are you saying you don’t have those today?

[04:53] Benji Okafor: We have most of it, but some of your routes are missing the “route_id” tag in the metrics. We saw that in the debugging. It means the dashboard aggregates across more traffic than we want.

[05:06] Lena Wu: That explains why your graph didn’t match ours by a bit.

[05:09] Rafael Mendes: Exactly.

[05:11] Hannah Rivera: To ground us: NorthBridge is Dedicated, multi-region, but the impact was us-east only, correct?

[05:18] Amit Desai: Correct. us-east-1. Europe was okay.

[05:22] Hannah Rivera: Okay.

[05:23] Paula Mendes: So for your case, we’d likely pilot in that region only. For thresholds: what do you consider a hard stop? Like p95 > what for how long before you want to rollback?

[05:35] Lena Wu: For the primary route, p95 above 1.2 seconds sustained for 5 minutes should be a rollback. But we also don’t want it to trigger during warm-up.

[05:45] Carlos Jimenez: Also depends on token length. If the prompt is long, p95 naturally goes up.

[05:50] Paula Mendes: Totally. Our SLO definitions are per route and we use “time to first token” and “end-to-end” optionally. For rollback we’re initially focusing on end-to-end and error rate. We can also support TTFT if that’s what you want.

[06:08] Amit Desai: We care more about TTFT because users feel the stall.

[06:12] Rafael Mendes: That’s doable but we need to ensure TTFT metric is reliably emitted for that route and streaming path.

[06:20] Benji Okafor: And that the query is stable. TTFT can be noisy during low traffic.

[06:24] Lena Wu: Which brings us to minimum traffic. We have low-volume tenants too. We absolutely cannot have auto-rollback for low traffic because of noise.

[06:33] Paula Mendes: Yep. The policy has a “minimum requests in window” gate. Example: only evaluate if at least, say, 200 requests in 10 minutes, or a minimum token count. We’re debating which is more robust.

[06:46] Carlos Jimenez: Token count is probably better.

[06:48] Rafael Mendes: We have token metrics, but they can lag by ~30-60 seconds depending on pipeline.

[06:54] Lena Wu: That’s okay if you’re not trying to decide in 10 seconds.

[06:57] Amit Desai: Our ask is rollback within 5-10 minutes of the regression starting, not 30.

[07:03] Hannah Rivera: Understood.

[07:05] Paula Mendes: Another guardrail is “must be worse than baseline.” So we’d compute canary p95 vs stable p95 and require delta above, say, 30% for the window.

[07:16] Lena Wu: That’s good.

[07:18] Jenna Park: But then audit. If an automated system changes traffic routing, we need logs: who/what did it, why, what data it saw.

[07:27] Benji Okafor: Yep. We emit audit events for policy changes and for rollbacks. The rollback event includes policy id, monitor ids, the computed verdict, and links to the graphs.

[07:39] Jenna Park: We’ll want those exportable to our SIEM.

[07:43] Hannah Rivera: We support audit log export for Dedicated. We can follow up with the exact event types, but yes.

[07:49] Rafael Mendes: Also, we’re adding an “unknown” state if monitors are stale or unavailable. We don’t want to rollback on missing data.

[07:59] Lena Wu: That’s crucial. We had an issue with Datadog—sorry, your metrics system—where queries returned null and another vendor rolled back everything. Not fun.

[08:09] Paula Mendes: Right. We’re deciding between fail-open and fail-closed behaviors. In most cases we will not rollback if we can’t fetch the monitor (unknown verdict). But you might still want an alert.

[08:22] Amit Desai: Alert yes. Rollback no.

[08:24] Rafael Mendes: +1.

[08:26] Hannah Rivera: Let me pause and make sure we cover the incident specifics too. Amit, what was customer-visible impact? Like, did you have SLA credits, did you page executives?

[08:36] Amit Desai: We had one customer ask why the assistant was “spinning.” We didn’t do credits, but we had a Sev2 declared internally. Our VP was in the thread. So, not catastrophic, but it’s a big brand risk.

[08:50] Carlos Jimenez: And dev velocity risk. If we can’t trust rollouts, we’ll slow them down.

[08:55] Hannah Rivera: Right.

[08:56] Benji Okafor: Can I ask a quick question: for the rollback behavior, do you want it to revert to previous stable automatically, or just freeze the ramp at current split?

[09:05] Lena Wu: Revert. If it’s bad, go back.

[09:08] Amit Desai: Yes. “Stop the bleeding.”

[09:11] Paula Mendes: That’s what we’re building: revert the canary/AB split to prior stable version. We also will log an event and notify Slack/on-call.

[09:21] Hannah Rivera: We can integrate with your Slack channel or your pager? We typically page Redwood on-call and notify customer channel depending on your preference.

[09:29] Lena Wu: Notify our Slack. Don’t page us unless it’s persistent.

[09:33] Rafael Mendes: Makes sense. We’re defining paging vs ticketing policy: auto-rollback events probably ticket unless it fails to rollback.

[09:43] Jenna Park: And manual override. If we’re doing a planned load test, we might accept temporarily higher latency. We need a way to disable auto-rollback.

[09:52] Paula Mendes: There will be a “pause” toggle and an “acknowledge” flow. Pause is like global disable for that rollout. Acknowledge is “I saw this and accept risk,” which can suppress notifications.

[10:06] Amit Desai: Okay.

[10:07] Hannah Rivera: Let’s dig into the policy knobs you care about most, and then we’ll talk timeline. Lena, you mentioned warm-up.

[10:13] Lena Wu: Yeah. We always see a little bump for 2-3 minutes when a new version starts due to cache warming and batching. We can’t rollback on that. So you need a warm-up window where you do not evaluate.

[10:26] Benji Okafor: We have a “grace period” after traffic starts. Default we’re proposing is 7 minutes, but that’s flexible.

[10:34] Carlos Jimenez: Seven seems high.

[10:36] Rafael Mendes: It depends on model size and your prompt distribution. But yes, we can tune.

[10:42] Paula Mendes: Another is cooldown: after a rollback triggers, we don’t want it to oscillate. Cooldown could be 30 minutes or until a new rollout starts.

[10:52] Amit Desai: Cooldown 30 is fine.

[10:55] Lena Wu: But what if the stable version is also bad because of an external incident? Then you’ll revert but still bad.

[11:03] Rafael Mendes: In that case auto-rollback doesn’t solve it, but it prevents a new bad canary from compounding. We’d still page on baseline SLO breach.

[11:12] Paula Mendes: That’s why baseline compare is important. If stable is already bad, we likely won’t rollback canary unless it’s worse.

[11:21] Lena Wu: Good.

[11:22] Carlos Jimenez: Another question: do you evaluate per tenant? Because we have a mix of premium and standard. Premium has tighter latency.

[11:30] Paula Mendes: Our policy model supports customer tier. Per-tenant thresholds are possible but not in the first iteration. It’s tier/route/region/model.

[11:41] Amit Desai: Tier is fine for us.

[11:43] Jenna Park: Per tenant could be a compliance concern anyway.

[11:47] Hannah Rivera: Okay.

[11:48] Paula Mendes: Now, the other big piece is monitors. The rollout controller will consume standardized monitors by identity. Benji can talk about what we need from your telemetry side.

[11:58] Benji Okafor: Yeah. In plain English: the system needs to ask, “What is p95 latency for route X, model version Y, region Z, tier T over window W?” and it needs a monitor id that maps to that query.

[12:13] Benji Okafor: So we’re standardizing labels and query templates. If labels are missing, you get the wrong number and then the system makes the wrong decision. So step 1 for pilot is we validate those labels exist and your dashboards line up.

[12:28] Lena Wu: Who owns that work? You or us?

[12:31] Rafael Mendes: Joint. We can fix missing labels in our metrics emission if it’s on our side. If it’s in your sidecar or your gateway config, you might need to update route naming.

[12:44] Carlos Jimenez: We don’t want to touch our gateway this quarter.

[12:47] Benji Okafor: I think it’s on our side, honestly. The route_id tag is coming from our routing layer. We can patch.

[12:54] Hannah Rivera: Great, we’ll track that.

[12:57] Amit Desai: Okay, timeline. When can we actually get this? Because we’re currently talking to Bedrock as a backup.

[13:07] Hannah Rivera: Yep, understood. Paula, can you give the product timeline at a high level?

[13:11] Paula Mendes: We’re targeting internal canaries first, then early-access customers in ~6-8 weeks. For you, I’d propose we put you in the early-access cohort with strict guardrails and feature flags.

[13:26] Lena Wu: Six to eight is… not ideal but okay if we can mitigate until then.

[13:31] Rafael Mendes: In the interim, we can set tighter alerting and a runbook with a faster path to revert split. Like a single command / console action rather than support tickets.

[13:42] Amit Desai: That would help.

[13:44] Hannah Rivera: We can also do proactive “hold at 10%” until a human says go, for the next rollout.

[13:52] Carlos Jimenez: Yes please.

[13:54] Paula Mendes: That’s basically manual gating. But yes.

[13:57] Jenna Park: For early access, what controls exist? Can we require approvals for policy changes?

[14:04] Paula Mendes: Policy changes are audited and can be restricted via RBAC. Approval workflow is not a full two-person rule in v1, but we can restrict to admin role.

[14:15] Jenna Park: Okay.

[14:17] Hannah Rivera: If it helps, we can document the change-control process: who can change policy, how we notify, etc.

[14:24] Amit Desai: We’ll need that.

[14:26] Lena Wu: I want to talk about false positives. We’ve had other systems trigger on low sample sizes. What’s your plan to avoid auto-rollback when a monitor is noisy?

[14:37] Rafael Mendes: Minimum traffic gate, plus requiring consecutive evaluation windows to breach. For example: breach for 2 out of 3 windows before action. That’s something we can configure.

[14:49] Paula Mendes: Yeah. The defaults we’re considering: 10 minute evaluation, check every 1 minute, require 5 consecutive bad verdicts, plus minimum requests.

[15:02] Carlos Jimenez: That’s like five minutes.

[15:04] Paula Mendes: Right.

[15:05] Lena Wu: Works.

[15:06] Amit Desai: But then what about the ramp? If you’re ramping to 35% in five minutes and it’s bad, you’re still harming customers.

[15:14] Benji Okafor: Good point. We can cap maximum canary percentage until health is “good” for some period. That’s not in v1 of auto-rollback, but we can do it as rollout policy: ramp slower.

[15:27] Paula Mendes: Also, we can set “minimum traffic” but that’s tricky: you want enough traffic to measure, but not enough to hurt.

[15:36] Lena Wu: Exactly.

[15:38] Paula Mendes: For your pilot, we can do: hold at 5% canary, evaluate health, and only then ramp. If it’s unhealthy, revert immediately.

[15:49] Amit Desai: That’s the right approach.

[15:51] Hannah Rivera: I’m hearing two tracks: near-term: slow ramps + better manual rollback. Mid-term: auto-rollback with the guardrails.

[16:00] Amit Desai: Yes.

[16:02] Jenna Park: Plus audit.

[16:03] Hannah Rivera: Yep.

[16:06] Carlos Jimenez: Can we talk about “who gets notified” if auto-rollback happens? We want to know it happened and why.

[16:13] Benji Okafor: The plan is: emit an event that our incident-bot posts in Slack. It includes: rollout id, version reverted to, reason (latency vs 5xx), the threshold and the observed value, and links to the rollout page and dashboards.

[16:28] Lena Wu: Good.

[16:30] Rafael Mendes: Also an audit log entry that your compliance team can pull.

[16:34] Jenna Park: Great.

[16:36] Hannah Rivera: Any other feature requirements we haven’t covered?

[16:41] Amit Desai: One: rate limiting. If there’s a global incident, we don’t want all tenants rolling back at once and causing more churn. Like a thundering herd.

[16:52] Benji Okafor: Yes. Executor will have per-tenant rate limits and global safeguards. And we will not allow one incident to trigger thousands of rollbacks concurrently.

[17:02] Rafael Mendes: Also, we’ll evaluate per rollout, so you’re not rolling back “stable” traffic, only the new candidate.

[17:09] Lena Wu: Okay.

[17:10] Carlos Jimenez: This might be out of scope, but quality regressions? Like if the model gets worse but latency is fine?

[17:16] Paula Mendes: Separate system. This project is latency/error SLO only.

[17:20] Carlos Jimenez: Got it.

[17:22] Hannah Rivera: Let’s capture some specifics for the pilot so we’re not vague. Which route should we start with? You mentioned “primary route.” Is that /v1/chat for your customer-facing assistant?

[17:35] Amit Desai: Yes. Our route is /nb-assist/chat.

[17:39] Benji Okafor: We might map that internally to a route id. We’ll confirm.

[17:43] Lena Wu: us-east-1 only, premium tier only.

[17:47] Paula Mendes: Great. And threshold: TTFT p95 > 1.2 seconds for 5 minutes? Or end-to-end?

[17:56] Amit Desai: TTFT p95 > 900ms is bad. End-to-end can be longer because token count.

[18:03] Rafael Mendes: We can do TTFT for rollback and end-to-end for alerting, or both.

[18:09] Lena Wu: Let’s do both, but only rollback on TTFT and 5xx.

[18:14] Paula Mendes: Okay. Error threshold: 5xx > what? 1%? 0.5?

[18:20] Lena Wu: If 5xx > 0.5% sustained for 5 minutes, rollback.

[18:25] Amit Desai: Agreed.

[18:27] Paula Mendes: Minimum traffic: at least 100 requests in 10 minutes? Does that sound right for premium tier?

[18:35] Carlos Jimenez: It’s more like 300-400 in peak.

[18:38] Lena Wu: 100 is fine.

[18:40] Benji Okafor: Warm-up grace: maybe 3 minutes.

[18:44] Lena Wu: Yeah.

[18:46] Paula Mendes: Cooldown: 30 minutes.

[18:49] Amit Desai: Yes.

[18:51] Paula Mendes: Baseline compare: require canary worse than stable by at least 25%.

[18:56] Lena Wu: That’s good.

[18:58] Hannah Rivera: Great. We’ll write that up and send back.

[19:01] Jenna Park: One more: can we get a “manual ack” that appears in the audit log? Like if we decide not to rollback.

[19:09] Paula Mendes: We’re adding “manual override / ack” events in audit. It will show who clicked it.

[19:15] Jenna Park: Perfect.

[19:17] Hannah Rivera: Before we wrap, Rafael, is there anything we learned from Tuesday that we should do immediately on Redwood side?

[19:24] Rafael Mendes: Two things. One, we think the regression was due to a misconfigured batching parameter for that model version, which increased queue time. That’s fixed in current stable. Two, the monitoring query we were using was aggregating across route families, which hid the spike for your route. That ties back to labels.

[19:43] Benji Okafor: And we’re adding a staleness check to ensure monitor values aren’t old. That prevents weird rollbacks.

[19:50] Lena Wu: Great.

[19:51] Amit Desai: Do you have a written incident report?

[19:54] Hannah Rivera: We have a draft internal post-incident. We can share a customer-facing summary: timeline, root cause, remediation. We’ll do that.

[20:03] Amit Desai: Please.

[20:04] Hannah Rivera: Okay.

[20:06] (small crosstalk)

[20:07] Carlos Jimenez: Can we also get guidance on how to set up the monitors? Or is that all on your side.

[20:12] Benji Okafor: We’ll provide the query templates and required tags. Some monitors already exist. For Dedicated, we can create them in our observability stack and expose the identities to the controller.

[20:23] Lena Wu: Okay. We just need visibility.

[20:26] Hannah Rivera: You’ll have visibility in Console: policy, current verdict (good/bad/unknown), rollback history.

[20:33] Amit Desai: That’s the biggest thing. We need a timeline view.

[20:36] Paula Mendes: Yep, there will be a history: breach detected at time X, decision at time Y, rollback executed at time Z, plus links.

[20:46] Jenna Park: And retention?

[20:48] Hannah Rivera: Audit retention depends on your package, but we can do 1 year for enterprise. We’ll confirm.

[20:55] Jenna Park: Okay.

[21:00] Hannah Rivera: I’m going to jump to next steps and owners so we leave with clarity.

[21:04] Hannah Rivera: One: I’ll send a recap email tomorrow with the proposed pilot policy values we just agreed: TTFT p95 900ms, 5xx 0.5%, window 5 minutes, grace 3 minutes, cooldown 30 minutes, min 100 requests, baseline compare 25%.

[21:22] Hannah Rivera: Two: Rafael will review your dashboards and validate freshness/lag and any missing labels. Benji will send the labeling checklist.

[21:30] Hannah Rivera: Three: Paula will share the draft policy semantics doc and we’ll get your feedback before we lock defaults.

[21:37] Hannah Rivera: Four: We schedule a pilot kickoff next week. Does Tuesday work?

[21:42] Amit Desai: Tuesday afternoon works.

[21:44] Lena Wu: Yeah.

[21:45] Hannah Rivera: Great. We’ll send invites.

[21:48] Hannah Rivera: Anything else you need from us before then?

[21:51] Amit Desai: Just the incident write-up. And the interim mitigation: slower ramps and a faster manual rollback path.

[21:59] Rafael Mendes: We can do the slower ramp immediately. For manual rollback, we can provide a runbook and a console link. Some of that is already possible.

[22:10] Benji Okafor: We can also add a “revert to previous stable” action in your rollout page for your account, under feature flag. Not promising by tomorrow but soon.

[22:20] Hannah Rivera: We’ll track it.

[22:22] Jenna Park: Thank you.

[22:23] Hannah Rivera: Okay, we’ll end early unless there are questions.

[22:27] Carlos Jimenez: One last nerdy question: is it burn rate or fixed threshold?

[22:31] Paula Mendes: For v1 we’re doing fixed thresholds with windows, but we’re evaluating burn-rate style as an option. For you, fixed thresholds probably map better to expectations.

[22:42] Carlos Jimenez: Works.

[22:44] Lena Wu: Thanks everyone.

[22:46] Hannah Rivera: Thanks all. Talk Tuesday.

[22:49] Meeting ended (recording stopped)

(Note: transcript includes minor inaccuracies due to automatic speech recognition.)
